title: Facta et Dicta Memorabilia
author: Valerius Maximus
source: Translated by Claude from phi1038.phi001.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.

passages.original: Quae minus admirabilia fere Eris Pamphyli casus facit, quem Plato scribit inter eos, qui in acie ceciderant, X diebus iacuisse, biduoque post quam inde sublatus esset, inpositum rogo reuixisse ac mira quaedam tempore mortis uisa narrasse.
passages.english: The case of Er of Pamphylia makes these things almost less wonderful. Plato writes that he lay for ten days among those who had fallen in battle, and two days after he had been taken up from there, when he had been placed on the pyre, he came back to life and told of certain marvellous things he had seen during the time of his death.

passages.original: sicut Porcius Cato L. Flamininum, quem e numero senatorum sustulit, quia in prouincia quendam damnatum securi percusserat tempore supplicii ad arbitrium et spectaculum mulierculae, cuius amore tenebatur, electo. et poterat inhiberi respectu consulatus, quem is gesserat, atque auctoritate fratris eius Titi Flaminini.
passages.english: So too Porcius Cato [removed] Lucius Flamininus, whom he struck from the roll of senators because in his province he had beheaded with the axe a certain condemned man, choosing the time of the execution to suit the wish and the entertainment of a wretched woman with whom he was infatuated. And [Cato] could have been held back by regard for the consulship which [Flamininus] had held, and by the authority of his brother Titus Flamininus.
passages.notes: The sentence begins elliptically ('sicut'), continuing a preceding sentence not supplied; the main verb (e.g. 'removed' / 'expelled') is implied by 'sustulit'.

passages.original: In Tullio uero fortuna praecipue uires suas ostendit, uernam huic urbi natum regem dando. cui quidem diutissime imperium obtinere, quater lustrum condere, ter triumphare contigit. ad summam autem unde processerit et quo peruenerit statuae ipsius titulus abunde testatur seruili cognomine et regia appellatione perplexis.
passages.english: In Tullius, however, Fortune showed her power above all, by giving this city as king a man born a household slave. It fell to him to hold power for a very long time, to close the *lustrum* [the census purification] four times, and to celebrate three triumphs. In sum, where he started from and where he arrived is amply attested by the inscription on his statue, in which a slave's cognomen and the title of king are intertwined.
passages.notes: Servius Tullius, sixth king of Rome.

passages.original: Nimis liberalis Archytae moderatio, temperatior Platonis: nam cum aduersus delictum serui uehementius exarsisset, ueritus ne ipse uindictae modum dispicere non posset, Speusippo amico castigationis arbitrium mandauit deforme sibi futurum existimans, si conmisisset ut parem reprehensionem culpa serui et animaduersio Platonis mereretur.
passages.english: Archytas' restraint was too indulgent; Plato's was more measured. For when he had flared up rather violently against a slave's offence, fearing that he himself might not be able to discern the right measure of punishment, he entrusted the decision about the chastisement to his friend Speusippus, thinking it would be disgraceful for him if he let it come about that the slave's fault and Plato's punishment deserved equal censure.

passages.original: Atque ut Theopompo quoque Spartanorum regi moderationis testimonium reddamus, qui cum primus instituisset ut ephori Lacedaemone crearentur, ita futuri regiae potestati oppositi, quemadmodum Romae consulari imperio tribuni pl.
passages.english: And so that we may also render testimony to the moderation of Theopompus, king of the Spartans: he was the first to establish that ephors should be elected at Lacedaemon, who would thus be set against the royal power, just as at Rome the tribunes of the plebs [were set] against the consuls' authority
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete; it continues in the following passage ("were set against the consular authority..."). "Tribuni pl." is the standard abbreviation for tribuni plebis.

passages.original: sicuti Liui quoque Salinatoris finiendarum simultatium inlustre consilium ignotum posteritati esse noluerunt: is namque, etsi Neronis odio ardens in exilium profectus fuerat testimonio eius praecipue adflictus, tamen, postquam eum inde reuocatum ciues collegam illi in consulatu dederunt, et ingenii sui, quod erat acerrimum, et iniuriae, quam grauissimam acceperat, obliuisci sibi imperauit, ne, si dissidente animo consortionem imperii usurpare uoluisset, pertinacem exhibendo inimicum malum consulem ageret.
passages.english: Just as they did not want the illustrious decision of Livius Salinator to end his feuds to be unknown to posterity either. For although he had gone into exile burning with hatred of Nero, having been ruined chiefly by his testimony, nevertheless, after the citizens recalled him from there and gave him [Nero] as his colleague in the consulship, he ordered himself to forget both his own temperament, which was very fierce, and the injury, which he had received in its gravest form, so that he would not, if he had chosen to share the command with a hostile mind, play the part of a bad consul by showing himself a stubborn enemy.
passages.notes: Nero is Gaius Claudius Nero, consul with Livius Salinator in 207 BC. The opening 'sicuti' continues a previous sentence not supplied.

passages.original: Mirifice etiam Thales: nam interrogatus an facta hominum deos fallerent 'ne cogitata quidem' inquit, ut non solum manus, sed etiam mentes puras habere uellemus, cum secretis cogitationibus nostris caeleste numen adesse credidissemus.
passages.english: Thales too [spoke] wonderfully: for when asked whether the deeds of men escaped the notice of the gods, he said, 'Not even their thoughts,' so that we might wish to have not only clean hands but also clean minds, since we would believe that a heavenly power is present at our secret thoughts.

passages.original: recte itaque Aeschines, cum propter iudicialem ignominiam relictis Athenis Rhodum petisset atque ibi rogatu ciuitatis suam prius in Ctesiphontem, deinde Demosthenis pro eodem orationem clarissima et suauissima uoce recitasset, admirantibus cunctis utriusque uoluminis eloquentiam, sed aliquanto magis Demosthenis, 'quid, si' inquit 'ipsum audissetis?' tantus orator et modo tam infestus aduersarius sic inimici uim ardoremque dicendi suspexit, ut se scriptorum eius parum idoneum lectorem esse praedicaret, expertus acerrimum uigorem oculorum, terribile uultus pondus, adconmodatum singulis uerbis sonum uocis, efficacissimos corporis motus.
passages.english: Rightly, then, Aeschines, when because of the disgrace of a court verdict he had left Athens and gone to Rhodes, and there at the city's request had read aloud, in a very clear and very pleasing voice, first his own speech against Ctesiphon and then Demosthenes' speech on behalf of the same man, and everyone admired the eloquence of both texts, but rather more that of Demosthenes, said: 'What if you had heard the man himself?' So great an orator, and so recently so hostile an opponent, so looked up to his enemy's force and passion in speaking that he declared himself an inadequate reader of his writings, having experienced the fiercest vigour of his eyes, the terrible weight of his expression, the tone of voice fitted to each word, the most effective movements of his body.

passages.original: Siciliae rector Hiero ad nonagesimum annum peruenit. Masinissa Numidiae rex hunc modum excessit, regni spatium lx annis emensus, uel ante omnes homines robore senectae admirabilis. constat eum, quem ad modum Cicero refert libro, quem de senectute scripsit, nullo umquam imbri, nullo frigore ut caput suum ueste tegeret adduci potuisse. eundem ferunt aliquot horis in eodem uestigio perstare solitum, non ante moto pede quam consimili labore iuuenes fatigasset, ac si quid agi ab sedente oporteret, toto die saepe numero nullam in partem conuerso corpore in solio durasse.
passages.english: Hiero, ruler of Sicily, reached his ninetieth year. Masinissa, king of Numidia, exceeded this limit, completing a reign of sixty years, and was remarkable above all men for the vigour of his old age. It is agreed, as Cicero reports in the book he wrote on old age, that he could never be induced by any rain or any cold to cover his head with a garment. They say also that he used to stand for several hours on the same spot, not moving his foot until he had worn out young men with a like exertion, and if anything had to be done sitting, he often stayed on his throne the whole day without turning his body in any direction.

passages.original: Biennio minor Xenophilus Chalcidensis Pythagoricus, sed felicitate non inferior, si quidem, ut ait Aristoxenus musicus, omnis humani incommodi expers in summo perfectissimae doctrinae splendore extinctus est.
passages.english: Two years younger was Xenophilus of Chalcis, the Pythagorean, but not inferior in good fortune, since, as Aristoxenus the musician says, he died free of every human ill in the highest splendour of the most perfect learning.

passages.original: Huius regis consummationem annorum minus admirabilem faciunt Aethiopes, quos Herodotus scribit centesimum et uicesimum annum transgredi, et Indi, de quibus Ctesias idem tradit, et Epimenides Cnosius, quem Theopompus dicit septem et l et centum annos uixisse.
passages.english: The completion of this king's years is made less wonderful by the Ethiopians, who Herodotus writes pass their hundred and twentieth year, and by the Indians, of whom Ctesias reports the same, and by Epimenides of Cnossus, who Theopompus says lived a hundred and fifty-seven years.
passages.notes: "This king" refers to a king named in the preceding text, which is not supplied. "septem et l et centum" is read as 157.

passages.original: L. uero Catilina in senatu M. Cicerone incendium ab ipso excitatum dicente 'sentio', inquit 'et quidem illud, si aqua non potuero, ruina restinguam'. quem quid aliud existimemus quam conscientiae stimulis actum reum a se inchoati parricidii peregisse?
passages.english: Lucius Catiline, when Marcus Cicero said in the senate that a conflagration had been kindled by him, said: 'I am aware of it, and indeed, if I cannot put it out with water, I will put it out with demolition.' What else are we to think of him than that, driven by the goads of conscience, he carried through the prosecution of himself for the parricide he had begun?
passages.notes: 'parricidium' here is treason against the fatherland.

passages.original: Sicut Anacreonti quoque, quem usitatum humanae uitae modum supergressum dum passae uuae suco tenues et exiles uirium reliquias fouentem unius grani pertinacior in aridis faucibus mora absumpsit.
passages.english: As [it happened] also to Anacreon: when he had gone beyond the usual measure of human life, and was nursing the thin and slender remnants of his strength with the juice of raisins, the too stubborn lodging of a single seed in his dry throat carried him off.
passages.notes: The sentence begins mid-thought ("Sicut... quoque"), referring to a preceding example not supplied. "passae uuae" = dried grapes, raisins (or raisin wine).
